Learn to make and alter clothing. This is a skill that will become invaluable in the next few years and you would be surprised how easy it can be. We have the advantage in that everything is too big rather than too small so you can always shrink it. Simple things like being able to take in a waist and hem a pant leg are getting ever more useful. I know that, for me, the time it takes to alter clothing is less effort than trying to find clothing that will fit, and I am not being sized out to the same severity as short people like your friend.

That's a really good idea. I've been interested in learning to sew for a while. Do you have any recommendations for people looking to learn? I can hand sew a button or hem something, but that's the extent of my abilities.

Just start simple. My first project was basically a giant bandana so it was easy straight lines. For alterations, take a shirt and turn it inside out. Cut out a crescent shape along the waist on both sides and sew it back together. Just like that you can take a shirt that is too big around the middle or a man's shirt and turn it into something nice. It only needs as much skill as doing a hem and you can hand sew it without any real cost investment. I only bought a machine last year because I figured it is time to get serious. From there, you can expand to altering sleeves if they are too loose or too square, and I had a go at shrinking the legs on a pair of pants that were too billowy. All of a sudden, you are doing intermediate sewing and it's not so scary. If you are really keen, there are templates you can find for making pieces from scratch. It sounds hard, but you are really only sewing two almost identical pieces together along the same lines. The collars and getting your measurements right are the fiddly parts, but you will have a custom-made item that fits perfectly exactly how you want it.

What you do want to look into are stitch patterns. In the waist especially, you obviously want some stretch so you can put the shirt on and take it off. There are stitch patterns that will give you that stretch while others are more rigid and better for a hem area. Another thing I learnt the hard way is knowing where to do something like a French hem so your joins are hidden, and more importantly, protected from a washing machine cycle that will tear all your hard work to pieces :/

It should really only take you about 20 minutes of reading on Google to learn enough to get you confident in starting. The rest is your imagination!
